headline: Sovereign and secure AI deployment is becoming a global standard as governments tighten data governance rules, creating a large enterprise market opportunity
reasoning: As governments establish AI governance frameworks, organisations need trusted service providers who can deploy AI in compliant, isolated environments — particularly avoiding reliance on public cloud. This is initially most pronounced in Europe with the EU AI Act, but management expects similar requirements to emerge globally including in Australia and other regions. The same sovereign AI principles also apply in defence contexts where privacy, confidentiality and isolated infrastructure are mandatory.
quote: The governments are there to keep us safe and to set the overall safeguards and expectations for governance. But organisations also need to know where can I access these technologies in a safe way? Not everyone has the capability to be able to work out how to do this in a way that is compliant but also supportive of what the organisation is trying to do. That's our role as a service provider. So we will take that template, we will take that model and we will look at other parts in the world and how we see how we can adapt that to each one of those regions, including this one here.
episode_title: Vection’s $20 million bet on secure AI

headline: Revenue $42M, EBITDA close to $4M with first positive full-year operating cash flow; share price near historical lows but strategy focused on sustainable moderate growth with European blueprint first
reasoning: Vection Technologies reported FY26 revenue of $42 million and EBITDA of close to $4 million, marking the company's first positive full-year operating cash flow. Luis Nejo described the result as purposeful rather than a turning point, emphasising the strategy has always been focused on moderate, sustainable growth. The company's European presence is anchored by its Italian engineering team and key relationships with Xerox and Dell, serving as a blueprint to be replicated in other regions. Despite the share price being near historical lows, Nejo expressed confidence that execution on strategy would eventually be recognised by the market.
quote: I wouldn't call that a turning point. This has been purposeful and we, we've been very clear in our what our strategy has been. It's not always easy, but our, our focus was to always have good moderate growth in in our numbers and to make sure that that's sustainable is always, is always the key and we're happy that we've we've managed to achieve that. Yeah, take a look at your share price. At the moment, you're close to historical lows. That must be disappointing for you, particularly given this news of the deal you've struck. What do you see as the catalyst for turning that around? Yeah. Look, we, we're the, the share price is an indicator, but we, we, we have our strategy, we're focused in our strategy and we have to execute on that. And we hope that the market recognises that when the result starts, start start speaking for themselves.
episode_title: Vection’s $20 million bet on secure AI

headline: $20M supply agreement with Italian telco Retelit to deliver secure sovereign AI services within European data centres, with a blueprint to expand globally
reasoning: Vection Technologies has signed a $20 million supply agreement with Retelit, an Italian telco with an extensive European data centre network. The deal involves providing AI infrastructure and secure sovereign AI services within Retelit's data centres, driven by European AI regulatory changes. Management sees this as a blueprint that can be replicated in other regions including Australia. The company brings AI expertise plus hardware deployment capability via a Dell partnership, enabling private cloud and on-premise AI deployments. FY26 showed revenue of $42 million and close to $4 million positive EBITDA, with the first positive full-year operating cash flow.
quote: The context of that arrangement is a very, very carefully constructed strategic partnership that is designed to deliver secure sovereign AI services within their data centre framework. So they have data centres and then have a lot of presence throughout Europe of those data centres in a heavily connected, interconnected way. So we are providing the AI infrastructure within those data centres. Data centres are there and obviously it's very topical today, but data centres are only as useful as the applications that you run in them. And we are providing a core set of services so that organisations can access AI in a safe way. It's driven out of the European AI changes and we will see similar things happen in other parts of the world.
